title: I asked Gemini to fix my Pixel issues; here's what actually worked
excerpt: Four everyday Pixel problems, and the exact settings Gemini pointed me to
content_html:
Published Oct 6, 2026, 11:00 AM EDT

Ali has spent more than a decade covering consumer technology, with a knack for looking beyond the specs, tinkering with software, and uncovering the bigger stories behind Android, Google, Apple, and everyday devices.

Over time, my Google Pixel had built up a handful of small annoyances, the kind of issues you notice at first but never really sit down to fix them properly.

Gemini has silently become useful for everyday troubleshooting like this, not only for asking trivia questions or writing emails. This brought me to ask about four separate issues instead of googling each one separately like I normally would.

Some of the answers were straightforward and immediately useful, but others only helped partially.

Either way, it beat digging through settings menus and guessing what might be causing each problem.

Battery drain had no obvious cause

Gemini found the actual culprit in battery usage

The first issue I discussed with Gemini was battery drain, which had gradually crept up enough that I couldn't pinpoint the exact reason.

I asked Gemini why my Pixel was draining battery significantly faster than usual and how I could figure out what was causing it.

It walked me through checking battery usage and flagged a power-hungry app running in the background. It also suggested changing my settings for that app instead of giving generic battery-saving tips.

I opened Settings > Battery > Battery usage, tapped the app Gemini flagged, and turned off the Allow background usage toggle under Manage battery usage. I did that for all the apps that I didn't use every day.

I tested the fix over the next few days to see if it made a difference, and it did. The improvement was not dramatic, but it was noticeably better than before I made the change.

It was a win for my Pixel and me.

Notifications had gotten completely out of hand

Fewer interruptions without going fully silent

With every new service I join, or when I'm surfing the web and creating accounts, my emails get flooded with promotional marketing material. The same approach applies to X accounts.

Over the past few years, I have followed many people on X and selected push notifications for most of them for news purposes. Now, it feels like my Pixel never catches a break, and neither do I.

I'd been putting this off for months, so I asked Gemini to find a solution. I asked the AI-powered assistant, "My Pixel gets too many notifications. What can I do to make it less annoying?"

Gemini pointed me toward finding the apps that are bringing in the most notifications through Notification History, along with app-specific notification categories.

Notification history, found under Settings > Notifications, showed me which apps were sending the most alerts, and each app's notification categories let me switch off only the ones I didn't need.

I tamed my notifications in the Settings app by turning off app-specific notifications and random notifications. By the end, the distractions and interruptions were reduced.

Now, I only receive notifications that matter to me and that I actually want to see and keep. This was more of a targeted fix than a blunt one.

My storage was full, and I didn't know why

A guided cleanup instead of random deleting

My Pixel's storage was getting full, and I wasn't sure what was taking up so much space. That's a frustrating spot to be in, because deleting the wrong thing is worse than deleting nothing at all.

Since all my photos are stored securely in Google Photos, I shouldn't worry about device storage filling up. Gemini walked me through it and explained which apps and files were taking up the most space and which of them were safe to remove.

In Settings > Storage, I could see what each app and file type was taking up, so I cleared the biggest ones.

That separation was useful for me, as I'm always unsure about app data and which of them are important. I freed up a hefty amount of space without deleting anything important.

My connection kept dropping, and nothing looked wrong

Gemini narrowed it down before I reset anything

The last issue was the most irritating one, because it came and went randomly. My Pixel always struggles to stay stable and keeps trying to switch between Wi-Fi and mobile data, even though my other devices work fine.

What made it hard to deal with was that nothing appeared broken, and it was hard to put my finger on what was going wrong.

Other devices kept working fine, which made me realize that the problem wasn't originating from the router.

I asked Gemini why my Pixel keeps losing its internet connection, even though other devices are working fine, and what I should check.

It asked me to change a few network settings and do the usual restarts and resets, but first it helped me narrow down the problem, which saved me from resetting everything.

I checked Wi-Fi and mobile data separately to see which one was causing the trouble. The fix was turning off Adaptive connectivity under Settings > Network & internet, along with the option to switch to mobile data automatically, so my Pixel stopped jumping between the two.

Gemini is now my first stop for fixes

None of these fixes were dramatic, and my Pixel doesn't feel like a different phone; it still functions the same and performs the same functions as normal.

What changed is that I now have a starting point for issues that used to mean a lot of scattered searching.

The battery fix was the most modest of the four issues, as it was better than before but not a major comeback. The notifications, storage, and connection fixes did what I needed them to do.

If you try this yourself, being specific in the question matters. I described what was happening and what I noticed, and the answers were more targeted than a generic troubleshooting list.

This holds real value for me.

Gemini doesn't have to solve everything for me; it just needs to tell me what the real problem is and where to look first. For me, that's precisely what it did pertaining to these four problems.
